sections.h2: Where is Columbus, Nebraska, and what is it known for?
sections.html:
Columbus is the seat of Platte County in east-central Nebraska, at the meeting point of the Loup and Platte rivers. Wikipedia places it about 85 miles west-northwest of Omaha and 75 miles northwest of Lincoln by road, and lists it as the eighth most populous city in the state with an estimated 25,248 residents in 2025.

Platte County's own history page says the Columbus Town Company sent agents from Columbus, Ohio in the summer of 1856, and that they marked the townsite when they reached the Loup River. The settlement soon had a mill, a hotel and a general store.

Inside the county, Columbus is by far the largest place. The NACO fact sheet gives it 24,028 residents in 2020 as a first-class city, against 905 in Humphrey and 667 in Newman Grove, and puts 23 percent of county residents outside any incorporated town. The county board meets every other Tuesday.

The county courthouse at 2610 14th Street has served since its dedication on June 26, 1922. A $1.76 million addition opened in September 1976 and holds the sheriff, the county board room, the treasurer and the courtrooms.

sections.h2: How did railroads and public power shape Columbus?
sections.html:
Railroads gave Columbus its start as a commercial center, and the Loup River power project gave it a second identity as a public-power town. The Union Pacific came through in 1866, and in 1881 a Burlington and Missouri River branch linked Columbus with Lincoln, which the county describes as turning the town into a railroad and commerce hub.

YearEvent in Columbus history
1856Columbus Town Company settles the site, May 28
1866Union Pacific Railroad reaches the town
1870First county courthouse completed
1881Rail line to Lincoln opens
1922Current courthouse dedicated
1934 to 1938Loup Project canal and power plants built
1946Behlen Manufacturing opens a factory on a former war-plant site

According to Wikipedia, the Loup Project is a 35-mile canal running from a diversion weir in Nance County to the Platte River, with one generating station near Monroe and another at Columbus rated at 45,600 kilowatts. At its peak, in October 1936, construction directly employed 1,352 people. In 1939 Consumers Public Power District was formed in Columbus, and by 1949 Nebraska had become the only state served entirely by public power.

Public power is still the local norm. The county fact sheet lists Cornhusker PPD, Elkhorn Rural PPD and Loup River PPD as providers in Platte County.

sections.h2: What drives the Columbus and Platte County economy today?
sections.html:
Farming, livestock and manufacturing lead the Platte County economy, according to the county's own history page. It names Lindsay Irrigation, known worldwide for center pivot systems, among the manufacturers.

Grain handling is concentrated in town too. The county lists ADM with 3,200,000 bushels of capacity and Frontier with 2,543,636 bushels in Columbus, plus elevators in Duncan, Humphrey, Lindsay, Monroe and Tarnov. Rail serves Columbus and several smaller towns. The same sheet counts 267 cattle producers and 465 crop producers in the county, which shows how much of the local income still comes off the land.

Columbus Public Schools is the public district, serving about 4,100 students from preschool through grade 12 according to the district. A second system, Columbus Catholic Schools, unites Scotus Central Catholic High School with St. Anthony, St. Bonaventure and St. Isidore elementary schools.

The county fact sheet also lists Lakeview Community Schools among the eight districts that reach into Platte County, and names Central Community College as the community college service area. Because district lines do not always match city limits, a seller should name the street address when a buyer asks which school a house feeds.

sections.h2: What do Platte County housing and income figures show?
sections.html:
Platte County is 72.0 percent owner-occupied, with 14,094 housing units counted in 2020 and a median household income of $72,335 in 2023. The county fact sheet cites the National Association of Realtors for a median home price of $224,780 in the fourth quarter of 2024.

  • Building permits in 2024: 71 for detached single-family homes and 27 for other housing units
  • Households in 2020: 13,313
  • Poverty rate in 2023: 9.9 percent
  • Registered voters in 2024: 20,823

Seventy-one detached permits in a county of about 34,000 people is a modest pace, so most home sales in Columbus involve existing houses rather than new builds.

sections.h2: Which Platte County offices handle property tax?
sections.html:
The Platte County Assessor, Treasurer and Register of Deeds all work from the courthouse at 2610 14th Street, Columbus, NE 68601. The county's fact sheet lists courthouse hours of 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. Monday through Friday.

  • The Assessor's page links the county's property search map.
  • The Treasurer bills and collects real estate and personal property tax.
  • The Register of Deeds records the deed that moves title.

The 2024 levy data on the fact sheet shows a county levy of $0.1846 per $100 of taxable valuation, $13,402,589 of county property tax, and $86,887,325 for all local governments on taxable valuation of $7,260,726,942. The county board's share is therefore about 15 percent of the total. On a $200,000 valuation the county levy alone comes to $369.20, and schools, the city and other districts add to that.

sections.h2: What about floodplain and well questions in Columbus?
sections.html:
Because Columbus sits where two rivers meet, a seller should expect buyers to ask about flood exposure. The county's online map viewer includes basemap layers labeled 2019 Flood and 2020 Flood.

The county fact sheet lists four natural resource districts with territory in Platte County: Central Platte, Lower Elkhorn, Lower Loup and Lower Platte North. It counts 1,297 rural drinking water wells and 2,150 irrigation wells. Any well capable of more than 50 gallons a minute must be registered and permitted through the local district.

The same fact sheet marks Platte County as not zoned, so county-level zoning does not apply outside the incorporated towns. City zoning and building permits still apply inside Columbus.

sections.h2: What does a Columbus seller owe at closing?
sections.html:
A Columbus seller owes Nebraska's documentary stamp tax, calculated under section 76-901 at $3.32 per $1,000 for transfers before 2032 and $2.32 after that. On a $200,000 sale the tax is $664.

Sellers of homes with up to four units also complete the written disclosure that section 76-2,120 requires, listing the condition of electrical, heating, water, sewer and other systems as the seller knows them. A purchaser who is denied the statement can sue for actual damages, court costs and attorney's fees, and must file within one year.

  • Request a payoff letter for any loan.
  • Ask the title company to show the tax proration line by line.
  • Keep receipts for any repairs you disclosed.

faqs.q: Which county office do I contact about taxes on a Columbus house?
faqs.a: The Platte County Treasurer at the courthouse, 2610 14th Street, Columbus, NE 68601. The Treasurer bills and collects real estate and personal property tax for the county.

faqs.q: Is Platte County zoned outside Columbus?
faqs.a: The Nebraska Association of County Officials fact sheet lists Platte County as not zoned. Inside Columbus, city zoning and building permit rules still apply.
Through public power. The county fact sheet lists Cornhusker Public Power District, Elkhorn Rural Public Power District and Loup River Public Power District as providers in Platte County.

faqs.q: What does Nebraska deed stamp tax cost on a Columbus sale?
faqs.a: The seller pays $3.32 for each $1,000 of value for transfers before January 1, 2032, so a $200,000 sale owes $664. After that date the rate drops to $2.32.

faqs.q: Do I have to disclose problems when I sell a Columbus house?
faqs.a: Yes for most one-to-four-unit homes. Section 76-2,120 requires a written statement of the property's condition as the seller knows it, delivered by the time a purchase contract binds the buyer.
